newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: PITCHED BATTLE OVER CZECH CROWN MAY WIPE OUT BAND.
newsitem.headline: PITCHED BATTLE OVER CZECH CROWN MAY WIPE OUT BAND.

text.p: A pitched battle over the Czech crown could come to a head in the coming days, and may lead to a widening or the elimination of the fluctuation band within which the central bank fixes the currency, analysts said.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) and speculators raised their week-long battle to new heights on Thursday, with hedge funds pushing the currency to record lows and the bank responding with interventions and other steps to choke liquidity.

The CNB moves -- which mirrored those taken by the Thai central bank in recent days as it successfully fended off speculators -- had an immediate effect, raising the crown to about 3.5 percent on the depreciation side of its basket parity from a record low of -6.4 percent earlier in the day.
But analysts said the central bank, with limited reserves and few effective options at its disposal, may be running out of room to manoeuvre.
"This is getting to the end of the line in terms of what you can actually do as a central bank," said Richard Gray, an emerging markets analyst at Bank of America in London.
"When your ammunition is used up -- there's still reserves certainly -- but the case for spending reserves on a lost cause is never clear and it all gets resolved quite quickly."
The crown, which has been under pressure for over a week, opened steady at about 2.7 percent on the depreciation side of its dollar/mark basket midpoint.

But speculators in London moved in soon afterward, pushing the crown to a record low of -6.4 against basket parity, forcing the central bank to step into the market directly in two waves for the third time in a week.

Dealers said the CNB had also been intervening in London by dealing directly with some foreign banks there, and put estimates of the cost of Thursday's intervention at between $500 million and $1 billion.
The central bank, with immediate effect, also agreed with large domestic banks to limit access by non-resident investors to the Czech money market.
CNB board member Ludek Niedermeyer told Reuters the central bank was also immediately closing all access to the Lombard credit facility, used by banks to borrow short-term funds.

"This is not a reaction to events only this morning but to the situation that non-residents are taking big positions on the money market. Basically this is increasing the volatility," Niedermeyer said.
The CNB also raised its one-week repo rate to 75 percent.

Dealers warned of the cost of maintaining the crown at current levels, adding the central bank may be forced to widen the +/- 7.5 percent band within which the CNB fixes the currency to allow it to lose value through market forces.

"We know that the economy is weakening and that the central bank is putting rates up, and that's bad news. I think the way out is for wider bands, I think they'll move to 15 percent bands," Stuart Parkinson, an emerging market analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.
Added Patria Finance's Vladimir Kriedl: "There is a feeling on the market that the crown is over-valued and our estimation is that it will go down about 10-15 percent in a few days."
"I would say the crisis should be resolved within a few days, maybe by the mid of next week I think we would see some outcome," he added.
Money market dealers said the central bank tightening moves ground trading to a virtual halt since no funds were available.
But analysts warned the moves were only short-term at best, and that when the central bank finally moves to ease its policies, the crown will come under fire again.
"I have said that the Czech crown is an accident waiting to happen, and it's now happening. I think that as soon as interest rates go down, the crown goes with them," Gray said.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
